Anselm of Canterbury 1033–1109 Archbishop of Canterbury: “faith seeking understanding”, the ontological argument, and Cur Deus Homo on why God became man.

Aquinas, Thomas 1225–1274 The "Angelic Doctor" of the medieval church, Aquinas synthesized Aristotelian philosophy with Christian theology, producing the most comprehensive intellectual system of the Middle Ages. His Summa Theologica remains the towering achievement of scholastic theology. He believed reason and revelation occupy distinct but complementary domains. His "Five Ways" for God's existence — from motion, causation, contingency, degrees of perfection, and design — remain central to natural theology. His synthesis of Aristotle raised questions about the relationship between nature and grace that the Reformers would contest vigorously. Luther's protest was partly against Thomistic categories. His concept of analogia entis (analogy of being) provided important vocabulary for how finite creatures can speak truly about an infinite God. Reformed thinkers are divided. Many, including Sproul, drew heavily on Aquinas's natural theology and arguments for God's existence. Others, following Van Til, resist the Thomistic nature/grace framework. All recognize him as an indispensable dialogue partner who cannot simply be dismissed. Summa Theologica (1265–1274)

Aristotle 384–322 BC Student of Plato and tutor of Alexander the Great, Aristotle ranged across logic, biology, ethics, politics, and metaphysics with unmatched systematic power. Where Plato sought transcendent Forms, Aristotle studied the observable world, finding purpose and order embedded in matter itself. His is a universe of causes, ends, and natures. His logic — especially the syllogism — became the intellectual backbone of medieval theology and remains the grammar of careful reasoning. His concept of the Unmoved Mover — a first cause that initiates all motion without itself being moved — was baptized by Aquinas into the Christian doctrine of God. His ethics of virtue and flourishing ( eudaimonia ) has been recovered by many Reformed thinkers as a complement to biblical ethics. Aristotle was the philosopher of the medieval synthesis and continues to underwrite much of Reformed philosophy via Aquinas. Sproul's classical apologetics owes much to Aristotle's logic and his cosmological arguments. Even those who critique Aquinas typically preserve Aristotelian logic as the tool of rational discourse. Nicomachean Ethics; Metaphysics (c. 350 BC)
Augustine of Hippo 354–430 Bishop of Hippo, whose theology of grace and whose Confessions and City of God shaped the whole Western church — and the Reformation.
Calvin, John 1509–1564 The Reformer of Geneva: the Institutes , the knowledge of God and of self, and the sense of the divine in every person.

Darwin, Charles 1809–1882 Though a naturalist rather than a philosopher, Darwin's On the Origin of Species (1859) triggered a philosophical earthquake whose tremors have never stopped. By proposing natural selection as the mechanism of biological diversity, Darwin offered a grand narrative of life without a Creator — purpose without a purposer, design without a designer. Darwinism dismantled the teleological argument for God in the minds of many educated Westerners. If apparent design can be explained by blind selection, the watchmaker becomes unnecessary. Applied to human beings, Darwinian evolution challenges the biblical doctrines of the image of God, the fall, and the uniqueness of humanity among creatures. Social Darwinism — the illegitimate extension of natural selection to ethics and society — fueled racism, eugenics, and the moral brutalities of the 20th century. Sproul devoted significant attention to Darwinism in Not a Chance and other works, arguing that chance cannot explain the ordered complexity of creation. The Reformed tradition insists that evolution as a complete metaphysical account of origins is incompatible with Scripture. Faithful Christians have differed over the age of the earth — the most natural reading of Genesis 1 is six ordinary days — but they cannot concede that humanity is merely a contingent accident. On the Origin of Species (1859); The Descent of Man (1871)

Descartes, René 1596–1650 The father of modern philosophy, Descartes set out to rebuild all knowledge on foundations that could not be doubted. His famous cogito ergo sum — "I think, therefore I am" — made the thinking self the starting point of all certainty. With this move, Descartes shifted the center of gravity in Western philosophy from God to the human mind. By grounding certainty in the individual thinking self rather than in God or Scripture, Descartes inaugurated the Enlightenment turn toward autonomy that would eventually undermine faith. He did argue for God's existence via a version of the ontological argument, and his rationalism left room for a Creator — but a God arrived at by unaided reason rather than received by faith. His radical mind-body dualism — res cogitans vs. res extensa — created philosophical problems still felt in discussions of the soul, free will, and human nature. Van Til identified Descartes as a pivotal figure in the story of unbelieving thought: the move from "God is" to "I think" as the starting point is, theologically, the move from Creator to creature as the measure of all things. Reformed epistemology (Plantinga, Wolterstorff) is in part a sustained response to the Cartesian project. Meditations on First Philosophy (1641)

Dewey, John 1859–1952 America's most influential philosopher of education, Dewey developed pragmatism into a comprehensive philosophy of experience and democracy. For Dewey, truth is not discovered but constructed — ideas are tools for solving problems, not windows onto transcendent reality. His educational philosophy, emphasizing child-centered learning and democratic community, reshaped Western schooling. Dewey's pragmatism dismantles the concept of objective truth. If truth is merely what works, Scripture's claim to be the Word of God becomes simply one useful story among many. His secular educational philosophy deliberately displaced religious and classical education, producing generations schooled to think without reference to God or transcendent moral standards. His naturalism — the view that only the natural order exists and science is the only reliable guide — permeates modern Western culture and academia. Many Christian critics have seen Dewey as a primary architect of the secular, relativistic educational culture that Christians now must resist and counter. The recovery of classical Christian education — with its grammar, logic, rhetoric, and grounding in Scripture — is in part a direct rejection of Dewey's legacy. Democracy and Education (1916); Experience and Nature (1925)

Foucault, Michel 1926–1984 French philosopher and historian of ideas, Foucault argued that knowledge is always entangled with power — that what a society calls "truth" reflects who controls discourse, not what is actually true. His genealogical method exposed how institutions (prisons, hospitals, schools, sexuality) construct and police "normal" behavior. He became the patron saint of postmodern critical theory. Foucault's reduction of truth to power is a direct assault on the Christian claim that God has revealed objective truth in Scripture. If all truth claims are power plays, the Gospel becomes merely ideology. His influence underlies the contemporary "hermeneutics of suspicion" — reading biblical texts not to understand them but to unmask the power interests they allegedly serve. His deconstruction of stable identity and human nature removes the anthropological foundation for biblical ethics, especially regarding gender and sexuality. Foucault represents the logical endpoint of a trajectory Sproul traced through Kant and Hegel — the progressive dissolution of objective truth. The Reformed response is not to retreat from engagement but to press the antithesis: if all is power, then Foucault's own critique is merely his power play, a self-refuting position. Christ alone is Lord of truth. Discipline and Punish (1975); The History of Sexuality (1976)

Hegel, Georg Wilhelm Friedrich 1770–1831 Perhaps the most ambitious philosopher in history, Hegel sought to show that all of reality is the self-unfolding of Absolute Spirit (Geist) through a dialectic often summarised (though rarely in his own words) as thesis, antithesis, and synthesis. History itself is the biography of God coming to self-consciousness through the human spirit. His philosophy dominated 19th-century European thought and spawned Marxism, existentialism, and liberal theology. Hegel's God is not the personal Creator of Scripture but an impersonal Absolute that needs the world to become itself — a pantheism in disguise that liberal Protestant theology eagerly embraced. His dialectical method — all truth emerges from conflict and synthesis — fueled both Marx's materialism and the liberal theology of Schleiermacher's successors, who dissolved doctrinal distinctions in the name of developmental progress. His recovery of history as meaningful — against Enlightenment atomism — opened space for recognizing that God acts in history, a theme Reformed biblical theology has developed. Sproul identified Hegel's pantheism as one of the most dangerous currents in modern thought. Hegel's God is not the holy, personal, triune God of Scripture; He is the world-process itself. Liberal Protestantism's collapse in the 19th and 20th centuries was largely a story of Hegelian dissolution of orthodoxy. Phenomenology of Spirit (1807); Philosophy of Right (1820)

Hume, David 1711–1776 Scotland's greatest philosopher and the most formidable skeptic of the modern era, Hume argued that all knowledge comes from sense experience, and that reason cannot establish causal connections, the existence of the self, or the reality of God. His critique of miracles — the probability of a miracle always being lower than the probability of witness error — became a standard objection to Christianity. Hume's critique of causation undermined the cosmological argument: we cannot infer from observed regularities to a First Cause, he argued, because causation itself is merely a habit of mind. His essay Of Miracles remains the most sophisticated secular argument against the historicity of the resurrection and biblical miracles generally. Hume's skepticism woke Kant from his "dogmatic slumber" and set the terms for all subsequent epistemology — both secular and theological. Sproul met Hume's challenge head-on in The Consequences of Ideas , arguing that Hume's own skepticism is self-undermining. Reformed apologists note that Hume's denial of the miraculous begs the question: it assumes the very naturalism that needs to be proved. Miracles are only impossible if God does not exist — and Hume cannot prove that without circularity. A Treatise of Human Nature (1739–1740); An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding (1748)

Kant, Immanuel 1724–1804 Born and buried in Königsberg, Kant never traveled more than a hundred miles from his birthplace, yet his mind ranged across the entire landscape of human thought. His "Copernican revolution" in philosophy — the claim that the mind does not conform to objects but objects conform to the mind — reshaped every subsequent discipline. His Critique of Pure Reason is the most important single philosophical text of the modern era. Kant declared that God, freedom, and immortality are beyond the reach of theoretical reason. We cannot know God as He is; we can only postulate Him as a moral necessity. This moved God from knowledge to faith — and to mere moral utility. His radical separation of the phenomenal (knowable) and noumenal (unknowable) world created a barrier between science and faith that liberal theology exploited by confining religion to the inner life of morality. His moral philosophy — the categorical imperative — preserved a universal moral law, which Reformed thinkers can engage as a point of contact with the image of God in moral reasoning. Sproul identified Kant as perhaps the single most consequential philosopher for Western Christianity's decline. By placing God behind an epistemological wall, Kant opened the door for Schleiermacher's subjectivism, Hegel's pantheism, and eventually the death of God. Reformed epistemology (Alvin Plantinga) is in large measure a sustained rebuttal of Kantian limits on theological knowledge. Critique of Pure Reason (1781); Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals (1785)

Kierkegaard, Søren 1813–1855 The "melancholy Dane" and father of existentialism, Kierkegaard reacted against Hegel's rationalistic system with a passionate insistence on individual subjectivity and inwardness. He described three stages of existence — aesthetic, ethical, and religious — culminating in the "leap of faith" beyond reason. His writings are by turns brilliant, ironic, and agonized. Kierkegaard's insistence that faith is personal, passionate, and existential — not a system — recovered something essential that dry rationalism had lost. Genuine faith involves the whole person before a living God. His "leap of faith" — choosing to believe despite and even against reason — was misread by 20th-century neo-orthodoxy (Barth, Brunner) to separate faith from history and objective truth, with damaging results. His ruthless attack on the cultural Christianity of his day — a comfortable, bourgeois, costless Christianity — remains a prophetic challenge to any comfortable church. Kierkegaard is a complex figure. Reformed thinkers appreciate his passion for genuine faith and his assault on empty formalism, but resist his anti-rational "leap." Faith, in the Reformed understanding, is not irrational but supra-rational — it rests on objective truth revealed in Scripture and confirmed by the Spirit. Genuine assurance requires objective grounds, not just existential intensity. Either/Or (1843); Concluding Unscientific Postscript (1846)

Locke, John 1632–1704 The father of classical liberalism and the philosopher most responsible for the political ideas of the American founding, Locke grounded political authority in natural rights, consent of the governed, and the social contract. A Calvinist by background, he argued for religious toleration and the reasonableness of Christianity — but on terms that would eventually prove corrosive to orthodoxy. His political philosophy of natural rights, limited government, and liberty directly shaped the American constitutional order — a framework within which Christianity has flourished and which Reformed thinkers have often endorsed. His epistemology — all knowledge from sense experience — laid groundwork for later empiricism and the marginalization of revealed religion. His Reasonableness of Christianity reduced the faith to a set of rationally demonstrable propositions, stripping it of mystery and preparing the ground for deism. Locke is a double-edged figure for Reformed Christians. His political legacy has provided the liberty within which the church has operated in the West. But his epistemology and his reductionist Christianity point in dangerous directions. The American founders who most honored him were often deists, not orthodox Christians — a fact that should give pause to uncritical Christian celebration of Lockean liberty. Two Treatises of Government (1689); An Essay Concerning Human Understanding (1689)
Luther, Martin 1483–1546 The Reformer of Wittenberg: justification by faith alone, the bondage of the will, and conscience captive to the word of God.

Marx, Karl 1818–1883 Co-author of the Communist Manifesto and architect of the most influential political philosophy of the 20th century, Marx saw all history as the story of class conflict driven by economic forces. His materialist inversion of Hegel — "it is not consciousness that determines life, but life that determines consciousness" — produced a secular eschatology promising liberation through revolution. Marx's "opium of the people" quip crystallized the view that religion is a tool of the ruling class to pacify the oppressed — a charge that has driven anti-Christian ideology from Soviet Russia to modern Critical Theory. His historical materialism removes God entirely from the explanation of human history, replacing Providence with impersonal economic forces. Liberation theology's identification of the Gospel with class struggle and political revolution is explicitly Marxist — and a fundamental distortion of biblical redemption. Marxism has often been described as a Christian heresy — a counterfeit eschatology that promises a heaven on earth achieved by human revolution rather than divine grace. It has a doctrine of sin (class oppression), a doctrine of salvation (the revolution), and a doctrine of the new creation (the classless society). The Reformed response insists that the root of human misery is not economic but spiritual, and that no political program can achieve what only the Gospel can. The Communist Manifesto (1848, with Engels); Das Kapital (1867)

Nietzsche, Friedrich 1844–1900 The most explosive and dangerous philosopher of the 19th century, Nietzsche announced the death of God — not as a metaphysical event but as a cultural one. Western civilization had killed God by making Him unnecessary, but had not yet realized it would also lose the moral foundations that only God could supply. His vision of the Übermensch (Superman) who creates his own values beyond good and evil was co-opted, grotesquely, by National Socialism. "God is dead, and we have killed Him." Nietzsche saw with devastating clarity that a secular culture cannot borrow the moral capital of Christianity indefinitely — once God goes, objective morality, human dignity, and meaning follow. His "will to power" as the fundamental drive of life underlies much 20th-century thought, from existentialism to Foucault's analysis of power/knowledge. Nietzsche's diagnosis is, paradoxically, one of the most powerful arguments for Christianity: if God is dead, the consequences are precisely as he described — nihilism, the collapse of meaning, the reign of the strongest. The Christian answer is that God is not dead; He is risen. Sproul engaged Nietzsche seriously, calling him a consistent atheist — far more honest than the secular humanists who deny God while clinging to His moral furniture. The Reformed apologist welcomes Nietzsche's challenge: yes, without God there is no objective morality, no human dignity, no hope. That is precisely why the Gospel is not optional. Christ is risen, and that changes everything. Thus Spoke Zarathustra (1883–1885); Beyond Good and Evil (1886)

Plato 428–348 BC The philosopher of philosophers, Plato's dialogues range from the trial of Socrates to the nature of love, from political philosophy to the immortality of the soul. His theory of Forms — that the visible world is a shadow of an invisible realm of perfect, eternal realities — gave Western thought its first rigorous account of transcendence. Whitehead was only slightly exaggerating when he called all subsequent Western philosophy "footnotes to Plato." Plato's world of transcendent Forms prepared the philosophical ground for Christian theology's account of God as eternal, immutable, and perfect — the source of all being, truth, and goodness. Augustine's conversion was mediated through Neo-Platonism. Plato helped him see that reality is not merely material — that beauty, truth, and goodness point beyond themselves to their divine source. Plato's dualism — body as prison of the soul — sometimes led Christian thinkers toward a denigration of the material world and the body that is not fully biblical. The resurrection of the body is a Jewish and Christian correction to this. Plato is a preparation for the Gospel, not the Gospel itself. Sproul appreciated the way Platonic transcendence counters materialism and opens minds to the reality of the invisible. But the God of Scripture is personal, not a Form — He speaks, loves, acts, and saves. Reformed theology receives Plato's insights while insisting on the biblical correction: the Word became flesh. The Republic (c. 375 BC); Phaedo; Timaeus

Plotinus 204–270 The founder of Neo-Platonism, Plotinus elaborated Plato's vision of transcendence into a mystical system centered on the One — the ineffable, absolutely simple source of all being from which everything "emanates" like light from the sun. His Enneads profoundly shaped later mystical traditions in Judaism, Christianity, and Islam. Neo-Platonism provided Augustine the conceptual vocabulary for speaking of a non-material God who is the source of all being, truth, and goodness — essential preparation for his conversion. The emanationist framework — reality flowing outward from the One and the soul's journey back to union with it — can blur the Creator-creature distinction that Scripture insists upon. The apophatic tradition (speaking of God by negation — what He is not) owes much to Plotinus and preserves a healthy sense of divine mystery before which words fail. Plotinus illustrates how far sincere reason can reach toward transcendence — and where it inevitably falls short. Without special revelation, the best philosophy achieves a mystical One, not a personal Father. The Reformed tradition affirms that God has revealed Himself as He is, in Scripture and supremely in Christ, and that general revelation leaves humanity without excuse but not without need of the Gospel. The Enneads (c. 253–270, compiled posthumously)

Rousseau, Jean-Jacques 1712–1778 The romantic rebel of the Enlightenment, Rousseau declared that man is born free but is everywhere in chains — civilization, property, and social institutions have corrupted an originally innocent human nature. His picture of natural man as innocent (popularly tagged the "noble savage," though the phrase is not his) and his "general will" as the source of political legitimacy fueled the French Revolution and modern progressive politics. Rousseau's doctrine of natural human goodness is a direct denial of original sin. If humanity is corrupted only by society, not by inherited guilt, then salvation is reform of social structures — not the cross. His sentimental, feeling-centered religion — conscience and nature as the path to God, doctrine as optional — prepared the ground for liberal theology's marginalization of revealed truth. The French Revolution, inspired by Rousseau, demonstrated what happens when the doctrine of sin is abandoned in politics: the Reign of Terror, not the Kingdom of God. The contrast with Calvin is sharp: where Calvin says man is radically corrupted by sin and can only be saved by grace, Rousseau says man is essentially good and corrupted by society. The 20th century — with its totalitarianisms, genocides, and moral collapse — is a laboratory test of both theories. The evidence overwhelmingly confirms Calvin and refutes Rousseau. Discourse on the Origin of Inequality (1755); The Social Contract (1762)

Sartre, Jean-Paul 1905–1980 The most famous philosopher of the 20th century's mid-century, Sartre's atheistic existentialism began with a simple premise: if God does not exist, then "existence precedes essence" — human beings have no given nature or purpose but must create themselves through their choices. His café philosophy of radical freedom and bad faith captured the post-war West's mood of dislocation and self-invention. Sartre's "existence precedes essence" is the philosophical charter for the contemporary conviction that identity is self-constructed rather than received — the root of the gender and sexuality revolution. His radical freedom — we are "condemned to be free," with no God, no nature, and no given purpose — produces anxiety (his nausea ) as the fundamental human experience. Sartre's honest despair — the "useless passion" of a freedom that cannot ground itself — is an inadvertent apologetic. The Reformed answer is that freedom without God is not liberation but vertigo, and Christ alone is the ground of genuine human dignity. Sproul saw in Sartre the most honest working-out of atheistic premises: if God is absent, meaning is self-made, identity is fluid, and death is the final word. The Christian answer is not sentimentality but history — the empty tomb, the risen Christ, the assured hope of resurrection. Sartre's despair is the logical end of every worldview that begins without God. Being and Nothingness (1943); Existentialism is a Humanism (1945)

Schleiermacher, Friedrich 1768–1834 The father of modern liberal theology, Schleiermacher sought to rescue Christianity from Enlightenment skepticism by relocating its essence in religious experience — the "feeling of absolute dependence" — rather than in doctrines or historical events. Raised in the Pietist tradition, he became the architect of a theology that traded the objective Gospel for the subjective inner life. By grounding religion in feeling rather than revelation, Schleiermacher opened the door to a Christianity in which doctrine is secondary, the cross is a moral example, and the resurrection is optional. Liberal Protestantism's progressive abandonment of orthodoxy in the 19th and 20th centuries flows directly from Schleiermacher's methodology: if experience is the judge of doctrine, no doctrine is safe. Schleiermacher's instinct that Christianity must be felt and not merely argued — that the Gospel addresses the whole person, not just the intellect — contains a truth the Reformed tradition also holds, even if his solution was fatal. Reformed critics have long identified Schleiermacher as the decisive wrong turn in modern Protestant theology. The Gospel is not primarily about religious experience; it is a declaration of what God has done in history — the incarnation, the atonement, the resurrection. Reformed preaching aims to produce genuine experience, but the experience is the fruit, not the foundation. On Religion: Speeches to Its Cultured Despisers (1799); The Christian Faith (1821)

Spinoza, Baruch 1632–1677 Excommunicated from his Amsterdam Jewish community at age 23, Spinoza constructed one of the most rigorous philosophical systems of the modern era. His God is identical with Nature — Deus sive Natura — an infinite substance of which mind and matter are two attributes. His Theological-Political Treatise pioneered the historical-critical method of reading Scripture as a human document. Spinoza's pantheism — God is everything and everything is God — directly contradicts the Creator-creature distinction at the heart of biblical theology. His historical-critical reading of Scripture as a historically conditioned human text, subject to the same analysis as any ancient document, launched the project that would dominate liberal theology: treating the Bible as a product of human culture rather than divine inspiration. His determinism — all things follow necessarily from the nature of God — raises questions that Reformed thinkers engage seriously: how to affirm both divine sovereignty and genuine human responsibility. Spinoza illustrates the trajectory of reason unmoored from revelation. His God cannot hear prayer, cannot be angered by sin, and cannot save. Reformed theology insists on the hard distinction: God is not the world; He is its sovereign Creator, distinct from and above His creation, yet intimately present by His Spirit and grace. Ethics (1677, posthumous); Theological-Political Treatise (1670)

Wittgenstein, Ludwig 1889–1951 Born into one of Vienna's wealthiest families, Wittgenstein gave away his inheritance and lived with monastic austerity, convinced that philosophy was not a body of doctrine but a therapeutic activity — the dissolution of confusion caused by language. He produced two utterly different philosophies: the early Tractatus , which tried to show the logical structure underlying all meaningful speech, and the late Philosophical Investigations , which dismantled his own earlier work. Both have profoundly shaped how thinkers approach religious language. His early Tractatus was seized upon by the Vienna Circle's logical positivists to argue that religious and ethical statements are literally meaningless — they neither picture facts nor are they logical tautologies. "Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent" became a weapon against theological language. His late philosophy of "language games" — the meaning of words is their use within a form of life — opened space for Wittgensteinian fideism (D.Z. Phillips, Norman Malcolm): religious belief is its own legitimate language game, not subject to defeat by scientific or historical criteria. The fideist reading cuts both ways: it protects faith from positivist attack but makes Christianity a self-enclosed form of life with no claim on outsiders — no universal truth, no real resurrection, no Gospel for all nations. This is not orthodoxy. Wittgenstein is a lens, not a gospel. Reformed epistemologists — particularly Alvin Plantinga — argue on their own grounds that belief in God can be "properly basic," not requiring external philosophical justification; but the Reformed tradition firmly resists the fideist conclusion: Christianity makes universal truth claims grounded in history (the empty tomb is either empty or it is not), not merely a language game for those already inside. Sproul insisted that faith seeks understanding — it does not retreat from it. Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus (1921); Philosophical Investigations (1953, posthumous)
Zwingli, Ulrich 1484–1531 The Reformer of Zurich: expository preaching through whole books, and the debate with Luther over the Lord’s Supper.

Boethius 480–524 Roman senator, philosopher, and Christian thinker, Boethius was the most learned man of his age. Falsely accused of treason, he awaited execution in a prison cell and wrote The Consolation of Philosophy — perhaps the most widely read book of the entire Middle Ages after the Bible. Lady Philosophy visits him in his cell and walks him through the great questions of providence, fate, free will, and the nature of true happiness. He was executed under the Ostrogothic king Theodoric. The Consolation of Philosophy shaped every major medieval thinker — Aquinas, Dante, Chaucer — and its account of God's eternal foreknowledge and human freedom provided the vocabulary for centuries of Reformed debate about providence and free will. His definition of eternity as "the complete, simultaneous, and perfect possession of unlimited life" ( nunc stans ) remains the classical theistic account of God's relationship to time — still cited by Reformed writers such as John Frame and Paul Helm in discussions of divine omniscience. His translations of Aristotle's logic into Latin preserved and transmitted Greek philosophy to the Latin West, making the entire medieval synthesis possible. Boethius is underread by evangelicals and invaluable. His prison-cell meditation on providence is not merely philosophy — it is a man clinging to God in the face of unjust death. His account of divine eternity (God sees all of time in one simultaneous present, so foreknowledge does not compel) is one of the most elegant answers ever given to the question of how God's foreknowledge relates to human choice. The Consolation of Philosophy (524); translations of Aristotle's Organon

Derrida, Jacques 1930–2004 Algerian-born French philosopher and the founder of deconstruction, Derrida argued that all texts are unstable — their meaning is endlessly deferred, never arriving at a fixed, authoritative sense. Words mean only by their difference from other words, not by pointing to stable realities. His reading of Western philosophy as secretly dependent on hidden, unexamined assumptions ("logocentrism") was enormously influential across the humanities and cultural studies. Deconstruction applied to Scripture produces a Bible with no stable meaning — every reading is as valid as every other, the author's intent is irrelevant, and the text's "authoritative" interpretation merely reflects the reader's power. This is the philosophical underpinning of much academic biblical criticism. His assault on "presence" — the idea that there is a stable meaning behind words — is an assault on the very concept of revelation. If the Word never truly arrives, God cannot truly speak. Paradoxically, some Christian thinkers (James K.A. Smith) have found in Derrida a useful critique of rationalist overconfidence, and have engaged deconstruction as a tool for exposing the idols of Enlightenment certainty — distinguishing this from wholesale adoption of his conclusions. Derrida is the philosophical machinery behind the claim that the Bible cannot mean anything definitive. The Reformed tradition's insistence on the perspicuity of Scripture — that God has spoken clearly and can be understood — is a direct counter-claim. Van Til's presuppositionalism anticipated the deconstructive move: without the God who speaks and whose words are anchored in His own eternal nature, all human language does indeed float free. The answer to Derrida is not cleverer hermeneutics but the living God. Of Grammatology (1967); Speech and Phenomena (1967)

Erasmus, Desiderius 1469–1536 The greatest scholar of the Renaissance and the most famous man of letters in Europe, Erasmus was a Catholic humanist who prepared the ground for the Reformation and then recoiled from it. His critical edition of the Greek New Testament (1516) gave Luther and the Reformers the textual tools they needed. Yet when Luther posted his theses, Erasmus refused to join — and the two men's great debate over free will became one of the most consequential theological exchanges in history. His Novum Instrumentum (Greek New Testament, 1516) — with its landmark correction of the Vulgate — directly enabled the Reformation's return to Scripture. Tyndale translated from Erasmus's Greek; so did Luther. His De Libero Arbitrio (On Free Will, 1524) argued that the human will retains some capacity to cooperate with grace — the precise point Luther demolished in De Servo Arbitrio (The Bondage of the Will, 1525). This exchange defines the fault line between Catholicism and the Reformation to this day. His satire of clerical corruption — In Praise of Folly — created the cultural atmosphere in which the Reformation's moral critique could be heard. As the saying went, he laid the egg that Luther hatched. Erasmus is the great "almost." He saw the corruption; he supplied the tools; he prepared the audience — and then stepped back from the decisive issue. Luther's reply to his free-will treatise, The Bondage of the Will , which Luther counted, with his catechism, among the only books of his worth keeping, is the definitive Reformed answer: the human will is not a middle ground between God and sin; it is in bondage until grace sets it free. Packer and Johnston's introduction to their translation of De Servo Arbitrio is essential reading on why this exchange still matters. Novum Instrumentum (1516); De Libero Arbitrio (1524)

Heidegger, Martin 1889–1976 The most influential and most controversial philosopher of the 20th century, Heidegger set aside traditional metaphysical questions about God and being and asked instead: what does it mean to exist? His Being and Time (1927) analyzed human existence ( Dasein ) as always already "thrown" into a world, oriented toward death, and called to authentic self-ownership in the face of inauthentic conformity. His later philosophy turned toward language as "the house of being." His enthusiastic membership in the Nazi party remains a permanent shadow over his legacy. Rudolf Bultmann, the most influential New Testament scholar of the 20th century, used Heidegger's existentialism as the framework for "demythologizing" the New Testament — stripping it of its supernatural elements and recasting the Gospel as a call to authentic existence. The resurrection became not a historical event but an existential possibility. Heidegger's analysis of "thrownness," anxiety, and being-toward-death infiltrated 20th-century theology so deeply that much Protestant liberal theology became existentialist anthropology with Christian vocabulary. His critique of technology and the modern reduction of all reality to calculable resources has been fruitfully appropriated by Christian thinkers (Albert Borgmann, Craig Gay) as a diagnosis of the spiritual shallowness of technological culture. Heidegger's influence on theology has been almost entirely corrosive. Bultmann's demythologizing — grounded in Heidegger — evacuated the Gospel of its historical content. The Reformed tradition insists that Christianity is not a structure of self-understanding but a report of events: the Word became flesh, was crucified under Pontius Pilate, and rose bodily on the third day. These are historical claims, not existential symbols. What Heidegger's framework cannot accommodate is precisely what Christianity cannot surrender. Being and Time (1927); "The Question Concerning Technology" (1954)

James, William 1842–1910 American philosopher and psychologist, brother of novelist Henry James, William James was the most celebrated thinker of his generation. He developed pragmatism — the view that ideas are true insofar as they work, insofar as they help us navigate life — and applied it to religion with extraordinary results in The Varieties of Religious Experience (1902), the most influential study of religious psychology ever written. For James, the test of religious belief is not metaphysical truth but its fruits in human experience. James's pragmatist account of religious truth — "God is real since he produces real effects" — reduces theology to therapy. A belief is "true" if it helps you live, not because it corresponds to reality. This opened the door to a Christianity evaluated by its psychological benefits rather than its factual claims. The Varieties of Religious Experience established the academic study of religion as the study of subjective experience — feelings, conversions, mystical states — rather than the study of God's objective self-revelation. This framing dominated 20th-century religious studies and continues to shape pastoral psychology. His precise, sympathetic descriptions of conversion, assurance, and mystical experience remain genuinely illuminating for pastors and counselors — even where his metaphysical conclusions are wrong. James is the philosopher of therapeutic religion. His pragmatism asks "does it work?" — the Reformed tradition asks "is it true?" These are not the same question, and confusing them has produced generations of Christianity evaluated by emotional satisfaction rather than fidelity to Scripture. Yet his Varieties repays careful reading: his descriptions of genuine religious experience — the twice-born soul, the sense of divine presence — often ring true even where his interpretation does not. The Varieties of Religious Experience (1902); Pragmatism (1907)

Justin Martyr c. 100–165 The first great Christian philosopher, Justin was a Gentile pagan who moved through Stoicism, Aristotelianism, Pythagoreanism, and Platonism before being converted to Christianity by an old man on the seashore who pointed him to the Hebrew prophets. He founded a philosophical school in Rome, wrote the first sustained intellectual defenses of Christianity addressed to the Roman Emperor, and was beheaded for his faith — hence "Martyr." His Apologies and Dialogue with Trypho are the earliest major works of Christian philosophy. His Logos theology — Christ is the eternal Logos (Word/Reason) in whom all rational beings participate — provided the first systematic bridge between Greek philosophy and Christian doctrine, enabling the church to engage Greek culture without capitulating to it. He argued that whatever truth the Greek philosophers found (Socrates, Plato) was a partial illumination by the universal Logos — seeds of the Word ( logos spermatikos ) scattered among all humanity. This "seeds of the Word" idea shaped how Christian missionaries have approached non-Christian cultures ever since. His First Apology contains the earliest detailed description of Christian worship — Sunday gathering, Scripture reading, preaching, Eucharist, collection — a priceless window into the 2nd-century church. Justin shows that engagement with culture and uncompromising fidelity to Christ are not opposites. His approach anticipates the Reformed cultural mandate: all truth is God's truth, and the church need not fear genuine human wisdom — while insisting that only in Christ does partial knowledge become saving knowledge. Sproul's willingness to engage philosophy seriously is in the tradition Justin established. The Logos who enlightens every person (John 1:9) is the same Logos who became flesh — and that changes everything. First Apology (c. 155); Dialogue with Trypho (c. 155–160)

Leibniz, Gottfried Wilhelm 1646–1716 German mathematician, diplomat, and philosopher — co-inventor of calculus alongside Newton — Leibniz was one of the supreme intellects of the early modern period. His philosophical system centered on the "monads" — indivisible, mind-like substances — and on his conviction that God, being perfectly rational and good, must have created the best of all possible worlds. He coined the word theodicy to describe the project of justifying God's goodness in the face of evil and suffering. He coined the term theodicy (Greek: theos + dikē , "God" + "justice") and gave his name for it to the ancient problem of evil — if God is all-powerful, all-knowing, and all-good, why does evil exist? Every subsequent Christian engagement with suffering and evil works within the framework he established. His argument that this is "the best of all possible worlds" — because a perfectly rational God would choose the best — was demolished by Voltaire in Candide after the Lisbon earthquake (1755), producing the modern assumption that suffering disproves God's goodness. His monadology preserved a genuine teleological universe — one of purpose and pre-established harmony — as an alternative to the purely mechanistic universe of Newton and Descartes. The problem of theodicy — Leibniz's bequest to theology — is answered in the Reformed tradition not by philosophical calculation but by Scripture and the cross. God is not obligated to create the best of all possible worlds by abstract rational necessity; He is sovereign and good, and His ways are not our ways (Isa. 55:8–9). D.A. Carson's How Long, O Lord? and Sproul's engagement with suffering take Leibniz's question seriously while refusing his rationalist framework. The cross is the only theodicy that actually satisfies. Theodicy (1710); Monadology (1714)

Ockham, William of c. 1287–1347 English Franciscan friar and the most formidable logician of the medieval era, Ockham is famous for "Ockham's Razor" — the principle that entities should not be multiplied beyond necessity, favoring simpler explanations. More consequentially, his nominalism — the view that universal concepts like "humanity" or "goodness" are merely names, not real metaphysical entities — shattered the Thomistic synthesis between faith and reason and prepared the intellectual soil from which the Reformation grew. Ockham's nominalism severed the connection between the created order and universal moral truths. If "goodness" is only a name, not a real property grounded in God's being, then God's commands become the arbitrary decrees of sheer will — the via moderna's voluntarism that terrified Luther. Martin Luther was trained in the Ockhamist tradition and reacted against it — but his reaction was powered by it. The Ockhamist insistence that Scripture and reason occupy separate domains cleared the ground for Sola Scriptura . His "Razor" — always prefer the simpler explanation — remains the most practically useful philosophical principle in intellectual history, widely used in science, theology, and apologetics. Ockham is the hinge between medieval and modern. His nominalism dissolved the synthesis Aquinas built, and the fragments fell two ways: toward the Reformation's Scripture-alone, grace-alone recovery, and toward the Enlightenment's reason-alone rejection of revelation. Luther fought his way out of Ockham's world, but the tools he used — the priority of Scripture over tradition, the freedom of God from philosophical necessity — were sharpened in the Ockhamist school. Understanding Ockham is understanding why the Reformation was not just religious but philosophical. Summa Logicae (c. 1323); Ordinatio (c. 1317–1318)

Origen of Alexandria c. 185–254 The most prolific and controversial theologian of the early church, Origen produced the first systematic Christian theology, the first critical edition of the Old Testament ( Hexapla ), and commentaries on almost every book of Scripture. He read the Bible with unmatched learning and creativity — and sometimes with alarming freedom, allegorizing where the text means to be taken literally. His speculations about the pre-existence of souls, the ultimate salvation of all beings (including Satan), and the spiritual nature of the resurrection were condemned as heretical after his death. His allegorical method of interpretation — every text has a literal, moral, and spiritual sense — shaped Eastern Christianity profoundly and influenced Jerome, Ambrose, and Augustine in the West. His On First Principles was the first systematic Christian theology — mapping the doctrines of God, creation, the fall, salvation, and Scripture into a coherent whole. Every subsequent systematic theology stands in his shadow. His doctrine of apokatastasis — the ultimate restoration of all things, including the devil — is the historical ancestor of modern universalism. It was condemned at the Second Council of Constantinople (553 AD) but never fully suppressed, resurfacing in every generation. Origen is a warning and a model simultaneously. His model: voracious engagement with Scripture, willingness to ask hard questions, and comprehensive systematic vision. His warning: what happens when speculative reason is given free rein over the text — the plain meaning is allegorized away, speculation multiplies, and the church ends up teaching what Scripture denies. The Reformed tradition's commitment to the literal-grammatical-historical sense of Scripture is, in part, a standing protest against Origenist excess. On First Principles (c. 220); Hexapla (c. 240); Against Celsus (c. 248)

Pascal, Blaise 1623–1662 Mathematical prodigy, inventor of one of the first mechanical calculators, pioneer of probability theory and hydraulics — and one of the greatest Christian apologists in history. Pascal's conversion (recorded in a piece of paper sewn into his coat, found after his death: "Fire. God of Abraham, God of Isaac, God of Jacob, not of the philosophers and scholars...") turned his genius toward the defense of the faith. He died at 39, leaving the unfinished fragments of his great apology for Christianity — published posthumously as the Pensées . Pascal's Wager — if God exists and you believe, you gain everything; if He doesn't exist and you believe, you lose nothing; therefore, belief is the rational bet — is the most famous argument in the philosophy of religion. More than a logical trick, it is a call to stop sitting on the fence and act on the stakes of eternity. His diagnosis of the human condition — that our craving is "an infinite abyss" that "can be filled only with an infinite and immutable object, that is to say, only by God himself" ( Pensées 425) — is popularly paraphrased as a "God-shaped vacuum" and is one of the most quoted ideas in Christian apologetics, anticipated by Augustine's "our heart is restless..." His "reasons of the heart" — "The heart has its reasons which reason does not know" — anticipated the fideist tradition while remaining orthodox: Pascal did not abandon reason but showed that the deepest realities (love, faith, God) exceed its grasp. Sproul loved Pascal and returned to him repeatedly. Pascal belongs to the Reformed tradition in spirit if not in formal confession — his Jansenist Augustinianism (total depravity, irresistible grace, predestination) put him in constant conflict with the Jesuit establishment. His Pensées are the most searching and honest account of what it means to be human before God since Augustine's Confessions . Every Christian apologist should be soaked in Pascal. Pensées (1670, posthumous); Provincial Letters (1656–1657)

Plantinga, Alvin b. 1932 Widely regarded as the most important Christian philosopher of the 20th and early 21st centuries, Plantinga taught for decades at Calvin College and Notre Dame and transformed Christian philosophy from a defensive posture into a confident engagement with the entire philosophical establishment. His free will defense, his modal ontological argument, and his Reformed epistemology reshaped the landscape of academic philosophy of religion beyond recognition. His free will defense — it is logically possible that God could not create free beings who always freely do right, therefore the existence of evil does not contradict the existence of an omnipotent, omniscient, all-good God — effectively defeated the logical problem of evil as a disproof of God's existence. Even atheist philosopher J.L. Mackie conceded the point. His Reformed epistemology ( Warranted Christian Belief , 2000) argued that belief in God can be "properly basic" — rationally held without requiring argument or evidence, grounded in the sensus divinitatis Calvin described. This dismantled the Enlightenment assumption that religious belief requires external proof to be rational. His evolutionary argument against naturalism (EAAN) — if our cognitive faculties evolved purely for survival, we have no reason to trust them to deliver truth, including the truth of naturalism itself — is one of the most powerful arguments against atheistic materialism ever formulated. Plantinga is Calvin's sensus divinitatis in philosophical armor. He demonstrated that the Reformed conviction — that knowledge of God is natural, not constructed; given, not achieved — is not a retreat from reason but its proper application. Sproul's classical apologetics and Plantinga's Reformed epistemology differ in method but agree in conclusion: the atheist, not the Christian, has the epistemological problem. Every Reformed pastor and apologist benefits from understanding what Plantinga has accomplished. God and Other Minds (1967); The Nature of Necessity (1974); Warranted Christian Belief (2000)
Schaeffer, Francis 1912–1984 Founder of L’Abri and critic of modern culture: Escape from Reason , How Should We Then Live? , and Christianity as “true truth”.

Singer, Peter b. 1946 Australian utilitarian philosopher, long Professor of Bioethics at Princeton, and the most influential living secular ethicist, Singer follows the logic of utilitarian ethics — maximize pleasure, minimize suffering across all sentient beings — to conclusions that most people find shocking: infanticide of disabled newborns is morally permissible; most affluent people are morally obligated to give until they reach the point of marginal utility; the life of a healthy chimpanzee may be worth more than a severely brain-damaged human infant. He is ruthlessly consistent. His denial of the intrinsic dignity of human life — personhood depends on cognitive capacities, not mere species membership — is the philosophical grounding for the abortion, infanticide, and euthanasia positions now becoming mainstream in Western law and medicine. His "animal liberation" movement (founded in Animal Liberation , 1975) logically requires that the image of God — which alone gives humanity unique moral status — be removed from ethical reasoning. If humans have no special dignity, the entire structure of biblical ethics collapses. His challenge to affluent Christians — "if it is in our power to prevent something bad from happening, without thereby sacrificing anything of comparable moral importance, we ought, morally, to do it" — is uncomfortably close to James 2 and 1 John 3:17. His conclusions are wrong, but the question is right. Singer is the clearest example of what consistent secular ethics looks like when it follows its own logic without the restraining influence of the image of God. The Reformed answer is not squeamishness but a counter-argument: human dignity is not earned by cognitive capacity — it is conferred by God, who made us in His image (Gen. 1:26–27) and redeemed us at infinite cost. Every human being — unborn, disabled, dying — bears that image and that worth. John Frame's Medical Ethics and Scott Rae's Moral Choices engage these questions from a Reformed and evangelical framework. Animal Liberation (1975); Practical Ethics (1979); Writings on an Ethical Life (2000)

Socrates c. 470–399 BC The founder of Western moral philosophy, Socrates wrote nothing — everything we know of him comes through Plato's dialogues and Xenophon's memoirs. He wandered the agora of Athens asking relentless questions, exposing the ignorance behind confident claims to knowledge, and insisting that "the unexamined life is not worth living." Convicted of impiety and corrupting the youth of Athens, he drank hemlock rather than compromise his calling. His courage before death was often recalled by early Christians. The Socratic method — the dialectical examination of ideas through probing questions — became the intellectual method of Christian theology from the church fathers through the scholastics to the present. Anselm, Aquinas, and Calvin all practice a fundamentally Socratic discipline of following arguments wherever they lead. His insistence that virtue is knowledge — that no one sins willingly, that evil is always a form of ignorance — was both corrected and deepened by Paul's account of sin as willful suppression of known truth (Rom. 1:18–32). The correction is precise: sin is not ignorance but rebellion. Justin Martyr argued that Socrates was illuminated by the pre-incarnate Logos — that his relentless pursuit of truth was a genuine, grace-given preparation for the Gospel. His death — unjustly condemned, accepting it for the good of his soul — haunted the early church and was explicitly compared to Christ's. Socrates shows how far honest, rigorous, humble inquiry can reach — and where it stops. He arrived at the immortality of the soul, the reality of moral truth, and the judgment of the wicked after death. He did not arrive at the resurrection, the atonement, or the name of Jesus. General revelation can create the hunger; only special revelation can feed it. The Reformed tradition honors genuine wisdom wherever it is found while insisting that Christ alone is the wisdom of God (1 Cor. 1:24). As recorded in Plato's Apology, Phaedo, Meno, and Republic (c. 399–360 BC)

Stoics and Epicureans 3rd century BC – 3rd century AD The two great popular philosophies of the Greek and Roman world — the ones Paul met face to face in Athens: “Some of the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers also conversed with him” (Acts 17:18). The Stoics, from Zeno onward, taught that a divine reason ( logos ) orders everything, and that the wise person accepts fate calmly and lives by virtue. The Epicureans, followers of Epicurus, taught that the gods are distant, the soul dies with the body, and the goal of life is a quiet, untroubled pleasure. Stoicism gave the ancient world, and later Christianity, a vocabulary of virtue, duty, natural law and self-control. Paul quoted a Stoic poet in Athens — “For we are indeed his offspring” (Acts 17:28) — as a point of contact. But the Stoic god is an impersonal reason woven into the world, not the personal Creator, and Stoic calm accepts fate rather than trusting a Father. Its renewed popularity today often offers self-mastery without grace. Epicureanism’s denial of providence, judgment and life after death is the ancestor of modern materialism: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die” (1 Corinthians 15:32). Paul’s speech on the Areopagus (Acts 17:22–31) is a model of engagement: he finds common ground in what his hearers already sense — that God made the world and is not far from us — and then confronts them with what neither school could accept: the call to repent, a coming judgment and a man raised from the dead. Calvin, who had studied Seneca closely, valued Stoic moral insight but rejected its fatalism; providence, he insisted, is the care of a personal Father, not the turning of a cosmic wheel. Seneca, Letters from a Stoic (1st century AD); Epictetus, Enchiridion (c. 125); Lucretius, On the Nature of Things (1st century BC)

Hobbes, Thomas 1588–1679 English philosopher who lived through the bloodshed of the English Civil War and concluded that, left to themselves, human beings live in a “war of all against all”, where life is “solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short”. In Leviathan he argued that people escape this condition only by handing their rights to an all-powerful sovereign. A thoroughgoing materialist, he held that everything, including the mind, is matter in motion. Hobbes took human sinfulness seriously — more seriously than many optimistic thinkers who followed — and saw that society needs restraint. Reformed readers recognise a distorted echo of the doctrine of depravity. His materialism and his grounding of morality in self-interest and the sovereign’s command, rather than in God’s law, laid foundations for secular political theory. His “social contract” — society as an agreement among individuals rather than a God-given order — shaped Locke, Rousseau and modern liberal democracy, for good and ill. Hobbes saw the problem of human evil clearly but proposed the wrong cure. Scripture does give government a sword to restrain evil (Romans 13:1–4), but it places rulers under God’s law, not above all law. The Reformed tradition — from Calvin’s teaching on lesser magistrates to Samuel Rutherford’s Lex, Rex (1644), published seven years before Leviathan — insisted that the law is king, not the king the law. The real answer to the war of all against all is not an absolute state but the new heart the gospel gives. Leviathan (1651)

Reid, Thomas 1710–1796 Scottish Presbyterian minister and philosopher, professor at Aberdeen and Glasgow, and founder of the Scottish “common sense” school. Reid answered the radical scepticism of his fellow Scot David Hume, who had argued that we cannot really know that the outside world, causes or even our own selves exist. Reid replied that certain beliefs — that the world around us is real, that our memories are generally reliable, that other minds exist — are rightly held without proof, as the starting points of all reasoning. Reid defended the reliability of our God-given faculties against scepticism, insisting that it is reasonable to trust our senses, memory and reason unless we have good grounds to doubt them. Common sense realism became the dominant philosophy at old Princeton Seminary and in American colleges in the nineteenth century, shaping Charles Hodge and B. B. Warfield. In the late twentieth century Alvin Plantinga and Nicholas Wolterstorff revived Reid as a forerunner of “Reformed epistemology”: belief in God, like belief in other minds, can be properly basic. Reid is one of the quiet heroes of Christian philosophy. His conviction that our minds are fitted by the Creator to know the world fits naturally with the doctrine of creation and with Calvin’s teaching on the sense of the divine. Critics, including Cornelius Van Til, argued that common sense realism gave fallen reason too much credit and too little attention to the effects of sin on the mind. But Reid’s answer to Hume remains powerful, and his influence on Reformed thinking is deep. An Inquiry into the Human Mind on the Principles of Common Sense (1764); Essays on the Intellectual Powers of Man (1785)

Voltaire 1694–1778 The pen-name of François-Marie Arouet, French writer, wit and the most famous figure of the Enlightenment. Voltaire attacked the power, intolerance and superstition of the church with satire, plays, histories and pamphlets, under the slogan Écrasez l’infâme — “Crush the infamous thing”. He was a deist: he believed in a Creator who made the world and then left it to run by natural laws, but rejected revelation, miracles and the deity of Christ. His novel Candide mocks the idea that this is the best of all possible worlds. Voltaire made mockery of Christianity fashionable among the educated, and helped turn Enlightenment “reason” into a weapon against revealed religion. His campaigns against real injustices — such as the torture and execution of the Protestant Jean Calas in 1762 — exposed cruelty done in the church’s name and promoted religious toleration. His deism, which keeps God at a distance and denies his involvement in the world, was a stepping stone from Christian faith to modern atheism. Voltaire was right to be outraged by persecution — the Huguenots had suffered terribly under French kings and bishops. But he attacked the gospel along with the abuses. Deism leaves us a God who made the world and abandoned it, and so no providence, no revelation and no Saviour. Scripture’s God is the one who “upholds the universe by the word of his power” (Hebrews 1:3) and has spoken finally in his Son. Voltaire’s mockery reminds Christians to answer with both truth and integrity, so that the gospel is not discredited by our conduct. Philosophical Letters (1734); Candide (1759); Philosophical Dictionary (1764)

Mill, John Stuart 1806–1873 English philosopher, economist and Member of Parliament, raised by his father in an extraordinary educational experiment — Greek at three, Latin at eight — and without any religion. Mill became the leading voice of utilitarianism, which judges actions by whether they produce “the greatest happiness of the greatest number”, and of classical liberalism. His essay On Liberty argues that the only legitimate reason to restrict a person’s freedom is to prevent harm to others. Utilitarianism measures right and wrong by results and happiness rather than by God’s law. It underlies much modern ethics, including arguments for euthanasia and embryo research. Mill’s “harm principle” — that the law should not forbid anything that harms only oneself — protects freedom of speech and conscience, but also drives the modern assumption that private morality is no one else’s business. He campaigned for the rights of women, including the vote, and against slavery, causes many Christians also championed. Mill rightly valued freedom of conscience, which Reformed Christians, having suffered persecution, also prize. But utilitarianism has no stable foundation: who defines happiness, and why should I seek the happiness of others rather than my own? Scripture grounds morality in the character and commands of God, and defines human flourishing as knowing and enjoying him. The harm principle, cut loose from a biblical view of the person, tends to reduce morality to consent — and cannot see that sin always harms the sinner and dishonours God. On Liberty (1859); Utilitarianism (1863)

Freud, Sigmund 1856–1939 Austrian neurologist and founder of psychoanalysis, who fled Vienna for London after the Nazi takeover in 1938. Freud argued that much of human behaviour is driven by unconscious desires, especially sexual and aggressive ones, shaped in early childhood and kept hidden by repression. Talking therapy, he believed, could bring them to light. An atheist, he explained religion as a “universal obsessional neurosis” and God as a projection of the human longing for a protective father. Freud’s account of religion as wish-fulfilment became one of the most popular arguments against faith: God is only what we wish were true. His insight that our motives are often hidden from ourselves echoes, in distorted form, the Bible’s teaching that “the heart is deceitful above all things” (Jeremiah 17:9). His view of humans as driven chiefly by sexual desire, and of guilt as a psychological problem rather than a moral reality, helped shape the sexual revolution and the therapeutic culture of the West. The wish-fulfilment argument cuts both ways: if belief in God could be a projection of our wishes, unbelief could equally be a projection of the wish that there were no Judge — as Freud’s own hostility to his father might suggest. Scripture agrees with Freud that we deceive ourselves, but locates the problem in sin against a holy God, not merely in repressed instinct. Guilt is not only a feeling to be managed but a real condition to be forgiven, and only the gospel can address it. Christian counselling has wisely learned to listen carefully, without adopting Freud’s view of the person. The Interpretation of Dreams (1899); The Future of an Illusion (1927); Civilization and Its Discontents (1930)

Chesterton, G. K. 1874–1936 English journalist, novelist, poet and debater — a large, cheerful man whose paradoxes and wit made him one of the best-known writers of his age. Raised in a vaguely Unitarian home and tempted by despair as a young man, Chesterton came to orthodox Christianity through reflection on wonder, gratitude and the strangeness of the world. He joined the Roman Catholic Church in 1922. His Orthodoxy and The Everlasting Man defended the faith with imagination and humour. Chesterton showed that orthodoxy is not dull but the greatest adventure — the sane and joyful alternative to the materialism, scepticism and pessimism of his day. The Everlasting Man answered the attempt to treat Christ as one religious teacher among many, and played a part in C. S. Lewis’s journey to faith. His defence of Christianity was explicitly Roman Catholic, including views on the church, the sacraments and Mary that the Reformed tradition rejects. Reformed readers will part company with Chesterton on the church, justification and the sacraments, and should read him with that in mind. But few writers have exposed so well the incoherence of modern unbelief, or recovered the sense of wonder and gratitude at the heart of the Christian view of creation. His instinct that the world is a gift from a good Creator, and that sin is the one Christian doctrine that can be empirically proved, makes him a valuable ally in apologetics. Orthodoxy (1908); The Everlasting Man (1925)

Russell, Bertrand 1872–1970 British philosopher, mathematician, Nobel laureate in Literature and public campaigner, one of the founders of analytic philosophy. With A. N. Whitehead he wrote Principia Mathematica , an attempt to ground mathematics in logic. Russell was an outspoken atheist; his lecture “Why I Am Not a Christian” (1927) set out the case against God, Christ and Christian morality that later atheists repeated. He campaigned for pacifism, nuclear disarmament and sexual liberalism, and was jailed twice for his protests. “Why I Am Not a Christian” popularised arguments — against the cosmological argument, against Christ’s moral character, and against Christianity as born of fear — that remain standard in popular atheism. His logical rigour and the analytic philosophy he helped found later became, unexpectedly, the main setting for a revival of Christian philosophy through thinkers such as Plantinga. His view that a meaningful life must be built “on the firm foundation of unyielding despair” in a universe without purpose expresses the bleak honesty of consistent atheism. Russell’s atheism was honest about its consequences: without God, human life is a brief accident in a meaningless universe. That honesty is itself an argument for the gospel. His objections to Christianity were often directed at a caricature — he criticised Christ’s teaching on hell while ignoring the cross — and his own moral passion for peace and justice had no foundation in his worldview. As Romans 1 teaches, the knowledge of God is suppressed, not absent; Russell’s life shows a man who could not stop asking the questions only God can answer. Principia Mathematica (with Whitehead, 1910–1913); Why I Am Not a Christian (1927); A History of Western Philosophy (1945)

Bultmann, Rudolf 1884–1976 German Lutheran New Testament scholar at Marburg, and one of the most influential biblical critics of the twentieth century. Bultmann argued that the New Testament presents its message in the “mythological” worldview of the ancient world — heaven above, hell below, miracles, demons, a literal resurrection — which modern people cannot believe. The task was to “demythologise”: to strip away the myth and reinterpret the message in terms of existentialist philosophy, as a call to authentic existence. Demythologising treated the miracles, the virgin birth and the bodily resurrection as myth, so that “Easter” became the rise of faith in the disciples rather than an event in history. His sceptical “form criticism” held that we can know very little about the historical Jesus, since the Gospels mainly reflect the beliefs of the early church. He did call people to a personal decision of faith in response to the preached word, and he opposed the Nazi-aligned “German Christians” as a member of the Confessing Church. Bultmann’s programme shows what happens when modern assumptions are made the judge of Scripture rather than the reverse. Paul did not regard the resurrection as a myth but as the heart of the gospel: “if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile” (1 Corinthians 15:17). Later scholarship has also undermined Bultmann’s historical scepticism: the Gospels are far closer to eyewitness testimony than he allowed. A faith that does not rest on what God actually did in history is not the Christian faith. Jesus and the Word (1926); “New Testament and Mythology” (1941); Theology of the New Testament (1948–1953)

Barth, Karl 1886–1968 Swiss Reformed theologian and the most influential Protestant theologian of the twentieth century. Trained in liberal theology, Barth was shocked when his teachers supported the German war effort in 1914, and turned back to Scripture. His commentary on Romans (1919, revised 1922) “fell like a bomb on the playground of the theologians”. He led the theological resistance to Nazism, drafting the Barmen Declaration (1934), and spent decades on his vast Church Dogmatics . His movement is often called neo-orthodoxy. Barth broke the hold of liberal theology, insisting that God speaks and humans listen, that theology must begin with God’s self-revelation in Jesus Christ, and that the church must not bow to the spirit of the age. The Barmen Declaration’s confession that Jesus Christ is “the one Word of God which we have to hear, and which we have to trust and obey in life and in death” remains a model of the church standing against tyranny. But Barth taught that Scripture becomes the Word of God when God speaks through it, rather than being God’s word in itself; he reworked election so that all humanity is elect in Christ, leaving his view open to universalism; and he rejected natural theology completely. Reformed theologians have long been divided on Barth. Many admire his Christ-centredness, his doctrine of God and his courage. But Cornelius Van Til argued that his “new modernism” used orthodox language with new meanings, and others have pointed to serious departures from the Reformed confessions: on Scripture, on election and reprobation, on the historicity of events such as the fall, and on the relationship between God’s revelation and history. Barth is best read critically: grateful for his recovery of a sovereign, speaking God, but holding firmly to the confessional doctrine of Scripture. The Epistle to the Romans (1919/1922); Church Dogmatics (1932–1967); Evangelical Theology: An Introduction (1962)

Tillich, Paul 1886–1965 German-American Lutheran theologian and philosopher, dismissed from his post by the Nazis in 1933, who went on to teach at Union Theological Seminary, Harvard and Chicago and became one of the best-known theologians in America. Tillich used a “method of correlation”: philosophy raises the questions of human existence, and theology answers them in symbols. God, for Tillich, is not a being who exists but “the ground of being” or “being-itself”, and faith is “ultimate concern”. By defining God as “being-itself” rather than a personal being who acts and speaks, Tillich moved theology toward a vague mysticism that many found indistinguishable from atheism. He treated the Christian story — creation, fall, incarnation, resurrection — as symbols of human existence rather than historical events. His analysis of anxiety and the human search for meaning in The Courage to Be was widely read, and he took seriously the questions modern people ask. Tillich shows the end of the road for theology that lets philosophy set the agenda. The God of Scripture is not an abstraction — “the ground of being” — but the living, personal LORD who says “I AM” (Exodus 3:14), who speaks, acts in history, loves and judges. Tillich’s symbolic reading empties the gospel of its content: if the resurrection is only a symbol, there is no good news. His questions about anxiety and meaning are real; the answer is not a symbol but a person, Jesus Christ, risen from the dead. The Courage to Be (1952); Dynamics of Faith (1957); Systematic Theology (1951–1963)

Dooyeweerd, Herman 1894–1977 Dutch legal philosopher at the Free University of Amsterdam, and the leading figure of Reformational philosophy, which grew from Abraham Kuyper’s vision of Christ’s lordship over all of life. Dooyeweerd argued that no thinking is religiously neutral: all philosophy rests on religious “ground motives”. He identified the ground motives of Greek thought (form and matter), medieval Catholicism (nature and grace) and modern humanism (nature and freedom), and set against them the biblical motive of creation, fall and redemption. Dooyeweerd showed that the claim of secular thought to be neutral and purely rational is itself a religious commitment — a powerful insight for Christian scholarship. His theory of “modal aspects” — the many irreducible dimensions of reality, from the numerical and physical to the ethical and faith — offered a Christian framework for every academic discipline. His work is notoriously difficult, and some Reformed theologians worried that his philosophy was too detached from the church’s confessions and too critical of traditional theology. Dooyeweerd’s great contribution was to take seriously Kuyper’s conviction that Christ claims every sphere of life, including thought itself. His critique of the “pretended autonomy” of reason parallels Van Til’s apologetics, though the two disagreed on many points. Through thinkers such as his brother-in-law D. H. T. Vollenhoven and later Reformational scholars, his ideas shaped Christian universities and organisations worldwide. He is hard going, but his central insight — that there is no neutral ground — remains vital. A New Critique of Theoretical Thought (1953–1958); Roots of Western Culture (1959)

Van Til, Cornelius 1895–1987 Dutch-American Reformed theologian who taught apologetics at Westminster Theological Seminary from its founding in 1929 until 1972. Van Til developed presuppositional apologetics: every person reasons from basic presuppositions, and there is no neutral ground between belief and unbelief. The Christian should not try to prove God from “neutral” premises, but should show that only the Christian worldview — the self-revealing triune God of Scripture — makes reason, science and morality possible at all. Van Til applied Reformed theology — the Creator–creature distinction, the authority of Scripture, the effects of sin on the mind — consistently to apologetics, refusing to grant that the unbeliever’s reason is neutral. His “transcendental” argument — that without God nothing makes sense, not even the logic the unbeliever uses — has been developed by Greg Bahnsen, John Frame and others. His style is dense and his arguments easy to misunderstand, and debates continue within Reformed circles between presuppositionalists and classical or evidentialist apologists such as R. C. Sproul. Van Til’s great insight is that the Bible must govern how we argue for the Bible. He took seriously Romans 1: unbelievers know God but suppress the truth, so apologetics is not about filling a gap in neutral information but about exposing the foundations of unbelief and calling people to repentance. Critics charge him with circular reasoning, and his writing is not easy. But many have found that his approach, rightly understood, gives the apologist both confidence and humility — confidence in the God who has spoken, humility because only the Spirit can open blind eyes. The Defense of the Faith (1955); Christian Apologetics (1976)

Frankfurt School (Critical Theory) founded 1923 A circle of Marxist thinkers at the Institute for Social Research in Frankfurt, including Max Horkheimer, Theodor Adorno, Herbert Marcuse and later Jürgen Habermas. Many fled the Nazis to the United States. They developed “critical theory”: not merely describing society but unmasking its hidden structures of power and domination in order to change it. Marcuse’s writings inspired the student radicals of the 1960s, and critical theory has spread through the humanities and social sciences. Critical theory treats truth claims, institutions and moral norms chiefly as expressions of power, and divides society into oppressors and oppressed — a framework that underlies much contemporary identity politics. Marcuse’s “repressive tolerance” (1965) argued that tolerance should be withdrawn from movements considered oppressive, an idea that has shaped later restrictions on speech. The Frankfurt thinkers did expose real dangers: the dehumanising effects of mass consumer culture, propaganda and the totalitarian state, which they had seen at first hand. Scripture agrees that power is often abused and that the oppressed matter deeply to God (Psalm 146:7–9). But critical theory offers a rival story of the world: its fundamental problem is oppression rather than sin, salvation is liberation through social change, and identity is defined by group membership. The gospel says all people, oppressed and oppressor alike, are sinners in need of grace, and offers a unity in Christ that overcomes every division (Galatians 3:28). Christians can learn from its critiques while rejecting its framework. Horkheimer and Adorno, Dialectic of Enlightenment (1947); Marcuse, One-Dimensional Man (1964)

MacIntyre, Alasdair 1929–2025 Scottish-born philosopher who taught in Britain and the United States, most of all at Notre Dame. After moving from Marxism to Christianity, he became a Roman Catholic in the 1980s. His landmark book After Virtue (1981) argued that modern moral debate is shrill and endless because we have inherited fragments of older moral traditions without the framework that made sense of them. He called for a recovery of the virtue tradition of Aristotle and Aquinas, lived out in communities. MacIntyre showed that the Enlightenment project of grounding morality in neutral reason has failed, leaving modern people with competing moral fragments and no way to settle disputes. He argued that rationality itself is rooted in traditions and communities — an insight that strengthened the case for distinctively Christian thought and practice. His final call to wait for “another — doubtless very different — St Benedict” inspired movements of Christian community, though his own tradition was Aristotelian and Thomist rather than Reformed. MacIntyre’s diagnosis is a gift to Reformed Christians: secular morality has no foundation of its own, and moral reasoning is never neutral — points Van Til and Dooyeweerd made in their own way.
