Reformed readers will want to ground virtue not finally in Aristotle but in God’s law and the renewing work of the Spirit, and to see the church, not merely local community, as the setting for a life of virtue. But his analysis of why moral debate has broken down is one of the most illuminating of our time. After Virtue (1981); Whose Justice? Which Rationality? (1988)

Taylor, Charles 1931– Canadian philosopher at McGill University and a Roman Catholic, known for his studies of the modern self and of secularisation. His monumental A Secular Age (2007) asks how the West moved from a world in 1500 in which it was virtually impossible not to believe in God to one in 2000 in which belief is one option among many, and often the harder one. He describes modern people as living within an “immanent frame” — a world understood without reference to anything beyond it. Taylor showed that secularism is not simply what is left when religion is subtracted, but a new set of assumptions and stories that shape how everyone, believer or not, experiences the world. His account of “expressive individualism” — the belief that each person must discover and express their own authentic self — explains much of modern culture, including sexuality and identity. His Catholic framework and his reluctance to make strong truth claims mean that his work diagnoses more than it prescribes. Taylor has become one of the most important guides for Christians seeking to understand the culture they live and minister in. Writers such as Carl Trueman ( The Rise and Triumph of the Modern Self ) and James K. A. Smith have drawn heavily on him. Reformed readers will want to add what Taylor leaves out — the clear proclamation of the gospel and the authority of Scripture. But to preach to secular people we must understand how they see the world, and Taylor helps us do that. Sources of the Self (1989); A Secular Age (2007)

Dawkins, Richard 1941– British evolutionary biologist and Oxford professor for the Public Understanding of Science, whose The Selfish Gene (1976) explained evolution from the perspective of genes. He became the most famous of the “New Atheists” — with Sam Harris, Daniel Dennett and Christopher Hitchens — after the 11 September 2001 attacks. His bestseller The God Delusion (2006) argued that belief in God is irrational and that religion is positively harmful. Dawkins made atheism popular and confident, presenting belief in God as a scientific hypothesis that has failed, and faith as belief without evidence. His argument that evolution makes design unnecessary, and that religion causes violence and should not be taught to children, shaped a generation of sceptics. The New Atheism provoked a strong response: Christian scientists and philosophers such as John Lennox and Alister McGrath engaged him publicly, and many found the debate drew them to examine Christianity seriously. Dawkins defines faith as believing without evidence, but that is not the biblical meaning: faith is trust in God, who has given evidence in creation, in history and supremely in the resurrection of Christ. His argument that a designer would need a designer misunderstands the God of Scripture, who is not a complex object within the universe but its uncreated Creator. Romans 1 explains the suppression of what creation reveals. Interestingly, Dawkins has more recently described himself as a “cultural Christian”, recognising the inheritance he cannot do without. The Selfish Gene (1976); The Blind Watchmaker (1986); The God Delusion (2006)

Butler, Judith 1956– American philosopher at the University of California, Berkeley, and one of the most influential figures in gender studies and queer theory. Drawing on Foucault and Derrida, her book Gender Trouble (1990) argued that gender is not something we are, rooted in nature, but something we do — “performative”, constituted by repeated acts shaped by social norms. She went further, questioning whether even biological sex is a stable, natural category. Butler’s theory that gender is a social performance rather than a given reality underlies much of contemporary gender ideology, including the separation of gender identity from biological sex. Her work treats the male–female distinction and the norm of marriage as social constructions to be subverted, regarding them as instruments of power that exclude those who do not fit. She rightly draws attention to the dignity of people who suffer violence and exclusion, a concern Christians should share. Scripture teaches that being male and female is not a social construction but a gift of creation: “male and female he created them” (Genesis 1:27). Our bodies are not raw material for self-invention but part of the good design of a loving Creator, and our identity is received, not performed. Christians must respond to people who struggle with their sex or sexuality with compassion and patience, rejecting both cruelty and the ideology that denies creation. The gospel offers what Butler cannot: an identity secure in Christ. Gender Trouble (1990); Bodies That Matter (1993)
